subsection: 1. The personal exercise and fitness area

points: The area is active and purposeful participation in a personally designed exercise and fitness programme.
The programme reflects the performer's own interests and goals.
The programme applies the principles of training to the chosen methods and exercises.
The aerobic choice is one method: continuous training, interval training, fartlek training, aerobics or step aerobics, spinning, or indoor rowing.
The second choice is one other conditioning and resistance activity: weight training, core stability or circuit training.
Only one of each is chosen, so each performance uses exactly two activities.
The warm-up lasts five minutes and comes first in the performance.
It includes a pulse raiser, an activity that gradually raises heart rate.
It includes mobility work and dynamic stretches, which move the joints and muscles through their range.
It includes movements that rehearse the development section, so the actions to come are practised first.
The development section lasts fifteen minutes and is the main part of the performance.
The cardiovascular section uses the chosen aerobic method.
The muscular strength and endurance section uses the chosen conditioning and resistance activity.
The muscular strength and endurance section can be organised as a circuit.
The cool-down lasts five minutes and comes last in the performance.
Intensity is reduced gradually rather than stopping abruptly.
Static stretches then cover the muscles used in the performance, each held still.

notes.h: Setting the goal: performance or health-related fitness
points: The programme aims either to improve performance in a physical activity or to improve health-related fitness.
A performance goal targets the fitness and skills that a chosen physical activity demands.
A health-related goal targets fitness that supports good health.
1. Set the goal.
2. Choose the methods.
3. Apply FITT (frequency, intensity, time and type) and the principles of training.
4. Choose the exercises.
5. Set the work and recovery periods.
6. Plan progression over weeks.
7. Record each session.
A progression makes an exercise harder in small steps, by increasing the load, repetitions, sets, duration or complexity.
Recovery can also be reduced to progress, by shortening the rest between sets or efforts.
An adaptation is an easier or harder version of an exercise, chosen so the programme suits the individual.
Press-up adaptations: on the knees or against a wall for an easier version, and with the feet raised for a harder version.
Technique and posture must be correct before the load is increased.
The load must be appropriate to the performer.
A spotter is used for heavy lifts.
Equipment is checked before use.
Fluids are taken to stay hydrated through the session.
The performer stops the exercise if there is pain or dizziness.
The space must be adequate for the activity.

notes.h: NCCA clarification: aerobic and anaerobic training
points: The NCCA clarification on curriculumonline.ie states that the training may be aerobic and/or anaerobic.
Aerobic training releases energy using oxygen; anaerobic training releases energy without oxygen.
A programme can therefore combine aerobic and anaerobic methods.

keyTerms.definition: Active and purposeful participation in a personally designed exercise and fitness programme that reflects the performer's interests, goals and the principles of training.
An activity that gradually raises heart rate at the start of a warm-up.
Stretching through controlled movement across the full range of a joint's motion.
Holding a stretched position still, without bouncing.
The fifteen-minute main part of the performance, made up of a cardiovascular section and a muscular strength and endurance section.
The five-minute end of a performance, in which intensity is reduced gradually and the muscles used are stretched statically.
A change that makes an exercise harder in small steps, such as more repetitions or sets, a larger load, longer duration, greater complexity or less recovery.
An easier or harder version of an exercise, chosen so that the programme suits the individual.
A partner who stands by during a heavy lift, ready to help if the lift fails.
An aim to improve the fitness and skills that a particular physical activity demands.
Fitness that supports good health, as opposed to the fitness and skill needed for one physical activity.

factCards.definition: A pulse raiser; mobility and dynamic stretches; movements that rehearse the development section.

factCards.term: Fifteen-minute development section: two sections in order
factCards.definition: A cardiovascular section, then a muscular strength and endurance section, which can be a circuit.

factCards.term: Five-minute cool-down: two steps in order
factCards.definition: A gradual reduction in intensity, then static stretches of the muscles used.

factCards.term: Designing a programme: seven steps in order
factCards.definition: Set the goal; choose the methods; apply FITT and the principles of training; choose exercises; set work and recovery; plan progression over weeks; record each session.
Correct technique and posture; appropriate loads; a spotter for heavy lifts; checked equipment; hydration; stopping for pain or dizziness; adequate space.

questions.prompt: Outline the structure of a personal exercise and fitness performance and describe the content of each part.
questions.model: The performance has three parts. The warm-up lasts five minutes and includes a pulse raiser, mobility and dynamic stretches, and movements that rehearse the development section. The development section lasts fifteen minutes and has two sections: a cardiovascular section that uses the chosen aerobic method, and a muscular strength and endurance section that uses the chosen conditioning and resistance activity, which can be organised as a circuit. The cool-down lasts five minutes: intensity is reduced gradually, then static stretches are held for the muscles used in the performance.

questions.prompt: Give two progressions and two adaptations for a press-up.
questions.model: Progressions: 1. Add repetitions over successive weeks, then add sets, making each change in small steps. 2. Reduce recovery, for example by shortening the rest between sets. Adaptations: 1. Press-up on the knees, an easier version for a performer who cannot yet manage the full exercise. 2. Press-up with the feet raised, a harder version.
